overview: Lombardy is a regional label here, not one continuous independent kingdom. The atlas assigns it changing patches around Mantua and other Lombard districts between 1650 and 1815. This card therefore presents dated examples from the region and names their local settings, rather than pretending that all belonged to the same ruler.

periods.title: Different neighboring governments
periods.summary: Mantua still had Gonzaga rulers, while Bergamo belonged to Venice. The regional name alone cannot identify the government of every mapped patch.

periods.title: Austrian and Venetian districts
periods.summary: Mantua passed to Austrian rule in 1708; Venetian institutions continued at Bergamo until 1797. Cultural and commercial connections crossed these political boundaries.

periods.title: Revolutionary change and Austrian restoration
periods.summary: French rule transformed much of the region. In 1815 an imperial patent established the Austrian Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia. This was a political reorganization, not the disappearance of Lombardy.

items.text: Mantua’s last Gonzaga ruler departed in 1707, and Austrian government followed in 1708. Later administrative reforms tied Mantua more closely to Milan. These changes matter because a label reading “Lombardy” can conceal quite different local histories and arrangements of power.

Bergamo’s great Venetian walls belong to a system of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century defences designed for the age of gunpowder. Projecting bastions changed the shape of a fortified city. They are evidence of military engineering and Venetian government, not proof of an independent Lombard kingdom.

A 1721 land record identifies a Sulbiate parcel owned by Giovanni Cottica as cultivated land with vines. This is a rare chance to look below the level of princes at a specific piece of working countryside. The later silk mill on the site should not be projected backward into 1721.

Mulberry growing and silkworm raising connected Lombard agriculture with textile production during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The Sulbiate site’s history records that wider setting before its later industrial use. A silk economy needed leaves and living caterpillars as well as skilled workers and machinery.

In 1715 a musician connected with the Polish court visited Stradivari’s Cremona workshop in connection with a commission for twelve violins. Fine instruments could move through international court networks. The workshop’s reputation was built from carefully made objects, not from a factory producing identical modern instruments.

Surviving Cremonese workshop materials include moulds, drawings, clamps, gouges, planes, files and calipers. A form marked G is associated with the 1715 Cremonese violin. These objects show planning and measurement behind the finished instrument: music began with plenty of quiet, patient woodworking.

The Cremonese violin’s label reads “Antonius Stradivarius Cremonensis faciebat anno 1715”: “Antonio Stradivari of Cremona made [it] in the year 1715.” This is the catalogue’s transcription of the actual Latin label, not a newly invented motto. Latin could advertise a maker inside a musical instrument.

Mantua’s Teresiana library opened to the public on 30 March 1780. A public library widened access beyond a private household’s shelves, although access to books still depended on literacy and circumstances. Its opening is a specific institutional achievement, not evidence that every child received schooling.

Mantua’s eighteenth-century scientific theatre hosted learned and civic gatherings as well as selected performances. Its 1767 contract excluded activities including gambling and acrobatics. “Scientific theatre” did not mean an auditorium full of laboratory benches: debate, ceremony and entertainment could share an architectural setting.

Bartolomeo Stefani’s L’arte di ben cucinare was printed at Mantua in 1662 and survives in a facsimile catalogued by the Warburg Institute. Its banquet material records elaborate culinary practice. A printed cookery book tells us about skilled cooking and display, not what every farming family ate each evening.

Volta’s battery, announced in 1800, stacked different metals with wet cardboard between them. Zinc, copper and salty moisture produced an electric current by chemical action. The key achievement was a continuing source of electricity, opening experiments that a brief spark alone could not sustain.

The 1815 imperial patent created the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia within the Austrian monarchy. The word “kingdom” on a document did not erase the region’s different towns, institutions or previous rulers. It marks a new governing arrangement after the upheavals of the French period.

ending.text: The map’s 1815 endpoint coincides with the creation of Austrian Lombardy-Venetia, not the death of a single long-lived state called Lombardy. Regional communities and crafts continued under changed government. The imported polygons remain too inconsistent to assign one precise political identity throughout this entry.
